title: New crash handler in macOS?
body: I wrote a test app with an intentional crash scenario and saw an unfamiliar crash-handler experience. This seems new to me. It is not itself a problem report; I am asking whether it is new and sharing it as an FYI. I attached a screenshot of what I saw.

symptoms_visible: When my test app intentionally crashes, an unfamiliar crash-handler interface and backtrace appear instead of only the crash output I expected.
N0.label: N0 unfamiliar crash handler reported

symptoms_visible: A one-line program that throws an unhandled managed exception invokes the Swift debugger on .NET 10 Preview 7 and macOS 26 Preview 7.
Launching the same test with the suggested backtrace-disable environment setting suppresses the Swift handler.
N1.label: N1 minimal reproduction and temporary suppression

symptoms_visible: The same Swift crash output appears on non-beta macOS 15.6 with .NET 10.
Downloaded .NET 8 and .NET 9 builds do not show it, and the downloaded .NET 10 Preview 6 build does not show it while Preview 7 does.
Locally built older runtime tags still show the Swift debugger, so the result does not follow the source revision cleanly.
N2.label: N2 scope and build comparison established

symptoms_visible: The official Preview 6 and Preview 7 executables report identical entitlements.
One official host without the backtrace has CS_HARD and CS_RUNTIME flags that are absent from a local host that shows the backtrace.
A runtime and host cross-built on x64 still show the same crash handler.
N3.label: N3 signing and architecture probes completed

symptoms_visible: The handler appears with dotnet run, but not when I invoke the built DLL directly with dotnet or when I pipe dotnet run so that it has no interactive terminal.
N4.label: N4 terminal-dependent behavior established

symptoms_visible: A maintainer reports that the mitigation makes .NET 10 behave like .NET 9, but I have not retested a build containing that mitigation on my own machine.
N_terminal.label: terminal mitigation shipped without reporter retest

question_patterns: Can you reduce this to a minimal unhandled-exception program and report the exact .NET and macOS builds?
Does a one-line managed throw produce the same crash interface?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. With .NET 10 Preview 7 and macOS 26 Preview 7, a one-line program containing throw new Exception("hello!") invokes the Swift debugger. I am not using a debug build of the runtime.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: A one-line managed throw only prints the normal .NET unhandled-exception output; the unfamiliar handler appears only in my original native-crash test.
The same one-line throw reproduces on a slightly newer macOS preview build.

question_patterns: Can you launch the same minimal test with the suggested runtime backtrace-disable environment override and report what changes?
Does the proposed environment override suppress the extra crash interface?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. Running SWIFT_BACKTRACE="enable=no" dotnet run disables the Swift backtrace handler for the same test.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The environment override makes no difference; the Swift debugger still runs.

edges.comment: Thread c5: participant1 reproduced the opening reporter's symptom with a minimal managed throw and tested the environment override. This affected operator is folded into the simulated user side; only the raw launch result is reported.

question_patterns: Can you test whether this also occurs on a stable, non-beta macOS release?
Is the behavior limited to the macOS 26 preview?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: It also occurs with .NET 10 on non-beta macOS 15.6. I attached a screenshot of that run.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: I cannot reproduce it on macOS 15; it appears only after installing macOS 26 beta.
It reproduces on macOS 15.5 instead of 15.6 with otherwise identical output.

question_patterns: What happens with official .NET 8 and .NET 9 builds on the same Mac?
Can you compare the crash output across supported .NET versions?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I cannot reproduce the Swift debugger with the official .NET 8 or .NET 9 builds, including on macOS 26 beta.

question_patterns: Can you compare downloaded Preview 6 and Preview 7 builds with locally built older tags?
Does a source revision bisection consistently separate working and failing builds?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The downloaded .NET 10 Preview 6 SDK does not end in the Swift debugger, while the downloaded Preview 7 SDK does. But a locally built Preview 6 tag does show it, and even my local v9.0.7 build shows it. The v9.0.7 run printed the .NET 9 framework description and then the Swift output; I attached that result. A source bisection does not cleanly separate good and bad revisions.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Both downloaded and locally built artifacts switch consistently at the same source commit.

edges.comment: Thread c10 and c13-c23: participant1 and participant5 tested stable macOS, official SDKs, and local builds. Their affected test systems are folded into the user side. The inconsistent build results are raw observations, not a conclusion about the cause. The reporter's c17 suggestion about two servicing PRs was rejected in c18 because the behavior was observed in an earlier commit; that fact is volunteered at N2.

question_patterns: Can you compare the code-signing entitlements on the official Preview 6 and Preview 7 hosts?
Do the working and failing official executables have different entitlements?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I compared the entitlements of the official Preview 6 and Preview 7 builds, and they are identical.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Preview 7 has a debug or runtime entitlement that Preview 6 does not have.

question_patterns: Can you capture the code-signing status flags for an official host and a local host that behave differently?
What raw CSOps flags do the two executables report?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: For an official .NET 10 Preview 7 process where I did not get the backtrace, CSOps reports CS_VALID, CS_GET_TASK_ALLOW, CS_HARD, CS_KILL, CS_ENFORCEMENT, CS_RUNTIME, CS_NO_UNTRUSTED_HELPERS and CS_SIGNED. For my local runtime build it reports CS_VALID, CS_GET_TASK_ALLOW, CS_KILL, CS_NO_UNTRUSTED_HELPERS and CS_SIGNED.

question_patterns: Can you repeat the product build through the x64 build pool and test the resulting runtime and host?
Does using an x64 cross-built host change the crash behavior?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I used a cross-built runtime and host, and it still crashed with the same handler.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The x64 cross-built runtime does not show the handler, while the arm64-built artifact does.

edges.comment: Thread c20-c28 and c34-c42: participant5 compared entitlements and CSOps output; participant7 performed the x64 cross-build experiment. These are measurement results from affected operators folded into one user side. Cross-building is a falsified diagnostic direction, not a persistent system fix.

question_patterns: Can you compare an interactive launch, direct DLL execution, and a launch whose output is piped?
Does the extra crash interface depend on how the process is attached to the terminal?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I can reproduce it with dotnet run, but not when I run the built app directly as dotnet bin/Debug/net10.0/app.dll. It also does not appear when I pipe dotnet run through another command.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The Swift handler appears identically for interactive, direct-DLL, piped, and CI-style launches.
The direct-DLL launch also shows it when I explicitly attach an interactive terminal, while noninteractive launches remain quiet.

edges.comment: Thread c33 and c37-c41: participant6 ran the launch-mode probes. Participant1 connected the raw no-TTY result to CI, but that conclusion remains engineer-side and is introduced by the final solution rather than placed in the user's answer.

solution.intent: Treat the output as the Swift runtime's intentionally activated backtrace handler, not as a new .NET managed crash UI or a macOS 26-only failure. Mitigate it from the native host at process startup by disabling Swift backtracing before Swift static initialization, while requiring custom hosts to apply equivalent early configuration.
solution.concrete_example: Have the native dotnet host set SWIFT_BACKTRACE=enable=no before the Swift runtime's static initializers execute. A host loaded later into another application cannot reliably do this after Swift initialization, so custom hosting scenarios must arrange the startup setting themselves. Ask the reporter to retest a current build containing the mitigation before declaring the issue resolved.
solution.inference_hint: Apple's confirmation that running the Swift handler was intentional, the requirement that SWIFT_BACKTRACE be set before Swift static initialization, and the explanation that CI did not expose the behavior because it lacks an active TTY came from maintainers and Apple guidance, not from the reporter's raw test output. The thread did not establish one source commit as the root cause; local and official build comparisons made source bisection unreliable.

edges.comment: Thread c44-c50: participant7 relayed Apple's guidance; participants7, participant8, and participant1 established that mitigation must occur in the native host before Swift initialization and discussed custom-host limitations. Participant9 later reported that a mitigation shipped, and subsequently said .NET 10 behavior matched .NET 9. The opening reporter never confirmed the result on their own machine, so the terminal state records relayed maintainer evidence and remains unverified by the reporter.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted cause at the certainty established by the thread: the unfamiliar output is the Swift runtime's backtrace handler being activated intentionally, not a new .NET managed crash handler and not a behavior unique to macOS 26.

Diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: the Swift-labelled minimal reproduction, suppression by the runtime backtrace environment override, reproduction on macOS 15.6, inconsistent official-versus-local build results, and terminal-dependent visibility.

Must recommend the host-side startup mitigation that disables Swift backtracing before Swift static initialization; setting it later from managed Main is too late, and custom hosts may need to arrange the setting themselves.
Must not present an x64 cross-build, a macOS upgrade, or the reporter's suggested servicing changes as the fix: those directions were contradicted by the in-thread tests.
Must explain that lack of an interactive terminal accounts for the behavior not appearing in CI, rather than treating CI silence as evidence that the issue is absent.

Must ask the reporter to verify a current build containing the mitigation before declaring resolution; the thread contains only a maintainer report that behavior was restored to the .NET 9 baseline, not an affected-reporter retest.

persona_hint.experience_level: Highly technical .NET contributor comfortable with preview SDKs, runtime builds, signing and release concerns; additional affected runtime engineers performing low-level build, entitlement, CSOps, architecture, and terminal probes are folded into the user side.
persona_hint.communication_style: Concise and collaborative, often framing observations as FYIs or questions; willing to run targeted experiments, share minimal repros and screenshots, and escalate release-risk concerns without overstating uncertain conclusions.
